Some poet's line: [the poet is Imru' al-Qays; another reading has "*tajawaztu ahrasan ilayha wa mashara*"; the full verse, from his Mu'allaqa, is "*ʿala hirasan law yasharuna maqtali*"] 
(I passed through guards and the terrors of a band of men)

It is also possible that *harasan* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) meaning: it was guarded with a very severe guarding.

God's words: ﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen; but whoever listens now finds a watching flame lying in wait for him.﴾ *Minha* means "from it," i.e., from the sky. *Maqa'id* are places in which one sits to listen to news from the sky. The meaning is that the rebellious jinn used to do this in order to hear news of the heavens from the angels and then convey it to the soothsayers (*kahana*), as explained earlier. So God guarded it when He sent His Messenger with burning meteors, and then the jinn said: ﴿whoever listens now finds a watching flame lying in wait for him.﴾ By *shihab* is meant the burning star, which has already been explained. It is said that the swooping down of stars occurred only after the mission (*mab'ath*) of the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is one of his signs.

The early scholars differed on whether devils were pelted before the mission, or whether this was something that happened at the time of the Prophet's mission (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi and a group said: the sky was not guarded during the interval (*fatra*) between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon them both, for five hundred years; it was only because of the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ). When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, they were prevented from all the heavens, and it was guarded by angels and meteors. I say: 'Ata' al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, as al-Bayhaqi mentioned. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: On the day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was made a prophet, the devils were prevented and pelted with meteors. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sabur said: The sky was not guarded in the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both; then when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the sky was guarded, the devils were pelted with meteors, and they were prevented from approaching the sky. Nafi' ibn Jubayr said: In the interval the devils would listen and were not pelted; then when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they were pelted with meteors. Something similar is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: No star was hurled since 'Isa was raised until the Prophet (ﷺ) was made a prophet, and then it was hurled.

It is also said: That occurred before the mission, but the pelting increased with the mission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as a warning about his condition. This is the meaning of His words *mulli'at*, i.e., the guarding of it was increased. Aws ibn Hajar, who was a pre-Islamic poet, said:

*Fa-nqadda ka-l-durri yatba'uhu ... naq'un yathuru takhaluhu tunuba*
(It swooped down like a pearl, followed by a dust cloud that rises; you would think it a tent-peg.)

This is the view of the majority. Al-Jahiz denied this verse, saying: "Every poem narrated with it is fabricated, and the pelting did not occur before the mission." But the view that pelting occurred is more correct, because of God's words: ﴿we found it filled with a severe guard and flaming meteors.﴾ This is a report from the jinn that the guard of the sky was increased until it was filled with them and with the angels. Also, based on what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: While the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting with a group of his companions, a star was hurled, and he said: [What did you used to say about such a thing in the pre-Islamic period?] They said: "We used to say that a great man dies or a great man is born." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [It is not hurled for the death or the life of anyone. But our Lord, glorified and exalted, when He decrees a matter in the sky, the bearers of the Throne glorify Him, then the inhabitants of each heaven glorify, until the glorification reaches this heaven. The inhabitants of the heaven ask the bearers of the Throne, "What has your Lord said?" They inform them, and each heaven is informed, until the news reaches this one. Then the jinn snatch it and are pelted, so what they bring is true, but they add to it.] This indicates that the pelting occurred before the mission.

Al-Zuhri narrated something similar from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, from Ibn 'Abbas. At its end it is said to al-Zuhri: "Was it pelted in the pre-Islamic period?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you think of His words, glorified is He: ﴿And that we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen; but whoever listens now finds a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾?" He said: "It was made stricter and its matter was intensified when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent." Al-Qutabi said something similar. Ibn Qutaybah said: It was so, but the guarding became stronger after the mission, and previously they used to steal hearing and were pelted in some circumstances; but when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, they were prevented from that altogether. This matter has already been explained in Surah al-Saffat [see vol. 15, p. 65] at His words: ﴿And they are pelted from every side, driven away, and for them is a constant punishment﴾ [al-Saffat: 8–9]. The *hafiz* said: If someone asks: How do the jinn expose themselves to burning themselves for the sake of hearing news, after this became known to them? The answer: God makes them forget this so that the trial is greater, just as Iblis forgets at all times that he will not become a Muslim, and God said to him: ﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Hijr: 35]. Were it not for this, the obligation (*taklif*) would not be realized.

*Al-rasad*: it is said that it refers to the angels, i.e., "and a guard (*rasadan*) of the angels." *Al-rasad* is the one who guards something, and its plural is *arsad*; in other places it may be a plural like *haras*, and its singular is *rasid*. It is also said that *al-rasad* is the meteor itself, meaning a meteor that has been set in wait for it, so that it may be pelted with it; thus it is *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *al-khabat* and *al-naqad*.

God's words: ﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance.﴾ That is, this guard by which the sky was guarded: is evil intended for those on earth, "or did their Lord intend for them *rashadan*," i.e., good. Ibn Zayd said: Iblis said, "We do not know whether God intended by this prevention to send down a punishment upon the people of the earth or to send to them a messenger." It is also said that this is a statement of the jinn among themselves before they heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth by sending Muhammad to them, for they will deny him and be destroyed by their denial as previous nations were destroyed when they denied, "or did He intend that they believe and be guided." So the evil and the right guidance here are disbelief and faith. On this view, they had knowledge of the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ), and when they heard his recitation they knew that they had been prevented from the sky to guard the revelation. It is also said: No, rather this was a statement they made to their people after they returned to them as warners, i.e., when they had believed, they feared that many of the people of the earth would not believe, so they said: "We do not know whether the people of the earth will disbelieve in what we have believed in, or will believe?"

**Tafsir of Surah al-Jinn, verses 11–12**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those who are otherwise﴾. This is the speech of the jinn. That is, some of them said to others, when they invited their companions to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ): "Before we heard the Qur'an, some of us were righteous and some of us were disbelievers." It was also said: "and among us are those who are otherwise" means "and among us are those who are below the righteous in righteousness." This second view is closer to the meaning than interpreting it as referring to belief and polytheism.

﴿We were paths, divided⦆ means separate sects. This was said by al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: "Different religions." Qatadah said: "Divergent desires." From this is the verse of the poet:

*The Withholder, the Expander, who guides by His obedience,*
*in the trial of people when their desires are divided.*

The meaning is that not all the jinn were disbelievers. Rather they were of different kinds: some were disbelievers, some were believers who were righteous, and some were believers who were not righteous. Al-Musayyab said: "We were Muslims, Jews, Christians and Magians." Al-Suddi, commenting on ﴿paths, divided﴾, said: "Among the jinn, as among you, there were Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on the sinner), Khawarij (Kharijites, secessionists), Rafida (Rafidis), Shi'a (partisans of 'Ali) and Sunniyya (Sunnis)."

Others said: the meaning is that after hearing the Qur'an we became divided: among us are believers and among us are disbelievers; that is, among us are the righteous and among us are believers who did not reach the level of righteousness. But the first view is better, because among the jinn there were those who believed in Musa and 'Isa, and Allah has told us about them that they said: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Musa, confirming what came before it﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 30). This indicates that a group of them believed in the Torah. This statement was also an exaggeration on their part in calling those whom they invited to belief. Moreover, there is no benefit in their saying, "We are now divided into believers and disbelievers."

*Tara'iq* is the plural of *tariqa*, which is a person's way or school of thought. That is, "we were different groups." It is said: "The people are *tara'iq*," meaning they follow various ways. *Qidad* is something like *tara'iq* and is an emphasis of it. Its singular is *qidda*. It is said: "Every path has a *qidda*." Its origin is from *qadd al-suyur*, which means cutting strips (of leather). Labid, lamenting his brother Arbad [[In MS z: (Murbad). In the other manuscripts: (Zayd), which is a distortion. The correction is from Sharh al-Qamus.]], said:

*The eye did not reach all its longing*
*on the night when the horses became like cut strips.*

Labid says: the eye did not attain, through weeping over Arbad, all that it desired on this night in which the horses are like strips of leather from the intensity of the march and exhaustion.

Another poet [[It is Labid, the author of the preceding verse, as in Fath al-Qadir of al-Shawkani.]] said:

*I said, while Zayd was bareheaded,*
*on the day the horses of 'Amr turned away in divided groups.*

*Al-qidd* (with a kasra) is a strip cut from untanned hide. It is said: "He has neither *qidd* nor *qihf*." *Al-qidd* is a container made of leather, and *al-qihf* is one made of wood.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And we thought that we would never escape Allah in the earth, nor could we flee Him by escape﴾. Here *zann* (thought) means knowledge and certainty. This is different from *zann* in His saying: ﴿And we thought that no human or jinn would ever speak a lie against Allah﴾ (al-Jinn: 5) and ﴿And they thought as you thought﴾ (al-Jinn: 7). That is, we knew through reasoning and reflection on the signs of Allah that we are in His grip and under His authority; we cannot escape Him by fleeing or by any other means. *Haraban* is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "fleeing."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 13–15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it and in Allah, and we affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) in his message.﴾ That is, the Qur'an. "And he (ﷺ) was sent to mankind and the jinn." Al-Hasan said: Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to mankind and the jinn, and Allah, Exalted is He, never sent a messenger from among the jinn, nor from the people of the desert, nor from among women. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. This meaning has already been discussed [see vol. 9, p. 274]. And in the Sahih: "I was sent to the red and the black," that is, mankind and the jinn.

﴿So whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither diminution nor oppression.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: he will not fear that his good deeds will be reduced or that his bad deeds will be increased, because al-bakhs is diminution, and al-rahaq is transgression and committing what is forbidden. Al-A'sha said:

Nothing benefits me apart from seeing her; Will a lover be cured if he has not committed a rahaq?

Al-wamiq is the one who loves; one says wamiqahu, yamiquhu, with a kasra, meaning he loved him, so he is wamiq. This is a statement that Allah related from the jinn, due to the strength of their faith and the soundness of their Islam. The common reading is fa-la yakhaf with a raf' (nominative), on the estimate of fa-innahu la yakhaf. Al-A'mash and Yahya [in manuscripts A and H: "Yahya from Ibrahim"] and Ibrahim read "fa-la yakhaf" with a jazm (apocopate), as a response to the conditional and dropping the fa'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the unjust.﴾ That is, after hearing the Qur'an we differ: among us are those who submitted and among us are those who disbelieved. Al-qasit is the one who deviates, the oppressor, because he turns away from the truth; al-muqsit is the just one, because he turns toward the truth. It is said: qasata, meaning he oppressed, and aqsata, meaning he acted justly. The poet said:

A people who killed the son of Hind by force, 'Amr, and they acted unjustly toward al-Nu'man.

﴿So whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance﴾, that is, they intended the path of truth and aimed for it, and from this comes tahharri al-qibla (seeking out the direction of prayer). [As for] the unjust [al-qasitun]

That is, those who deviate from the path of truth and faith, they are fuel for Hell (ḥaṭaban).

That is, firewood. And His saying: "they were"

That is, in the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: "And that if they had remained upright on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink."** This is from the speech of Allah, meaning: if these disbelievers had believed, We would have expanded their provision in this world and widened their sustenance for them. This is understood as a matter of revelation, meaning: it was revealed to me that if they had remained upright.

Ibn Bahr mentioned: everything in this surah that has the heavy, kasrah-marked *inna* is a report of the words of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an and then returned to their people as warners. Everything in it that has the light, fatha-marked *anna* is revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads the particles with kasrah but reads *wa-an law istaqamu* with fatha, has implied a complete oath, its meaning being: "By Allah, if they had remained upright on the path," just as it is said in speech: "By Allah, if you had stood, I would have stood," and "By Allah, if you stood, I would stand." The poet said:

*"Indeed, by Allah, if only I were free,*
*and you are neither free nor a freed slave."*

Whoever reads with fatha the letter before the light *an* (the *anna* of revelation), makes it coordinate with *anna hu* ("that it") after "it was revealed to me," and *wa-an law istaqamu*, or with "we believed in it and in that if they had remained upright." [[In the margin of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi: (Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever recites with kasrah in what came before and with fatha in "and that if they had remained upright," implies an oath whose estimate is: "By Allah, that if they had remained upright on the path." Or he makes it coordinate with "that he listened," or with "we believed in it." On this view, everything mentioned before is parenthetical between the coordinated and that to which it is coordinated.)]]

Whoever reads all the particles with kasrah up to the light *an* may coordinate the light *an* with "it was revealed to me" or with "we believed in it," and dispense with implying an oath.

The reading of the majority (*qira'at al-'ammah*, the standard recitation) is with kasrah on the *waw* of *law* because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Wththab and al-A'mash read it with a *damma* on the *waw*.

**"And abundant water"**: that is, plentiful and copious. They had been deprived of rain for seven years. It is said: "The spring gushed (*ghadaqat al-'ayn*), it gushes, so it is *ghadiqah*," when its water becomes abundant.

It was also said: the intended meaning is all of creation, that is, if they had remained upright on the path, the path of truth, faith, and guidance, and had been believers and obedient, We would have given them abundant water to drink, **"that We might test them therein,"** that is, that We might examine them, how they would give thanks for those blessings.

Umar said regarding this verse: "Wherever water is, wealth is; and wherever wealth is, there is trial." So the meaning of "We would have given them to drink" is: We would have expanded provision for them in this world. The abundant, copious water was used as a parable for that, because all good and provision come through rain. So it stood in its place, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been godfearing, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], and His words: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], meaning by rain. And Allah knows best.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Muqatil, 'Atiyyah, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and al-Hasan said: "By Allah, the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were listeners and obedient. Then the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, al-Muqawqis, and al-Najashi were opened to them, and they were tested by them, so they rose against their leader and killed him," meaning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him).

Al-Kalbi and others said: "And that if they had remained upright on the path in which they were, that is, in disbelief, and all of them had been disbelievers, We would have expanded their provisions as a stratagem against them and a gradual leading toward destruction, until they become tempted by them, and We punish them with them in this world and the Hereafter." The first view is closer to correct, because "the path" is defined with the article (*al-*), so it is most fitting that their path be the path of guidance, and because uprightness (*istiqamah*) is only with guidance.

Regarding his turning away from it there are two views: the first, from accepting it, if it is said that this is about the people of disbelief; the second, from acting upon it, if it is said that it is about the believers. The rest read *naslukhu* with *nun*. It is also narrated from Muslim ibn Jundab that the *nun* was read with *damma* and the *lam* with *kasrah*. **"A severe punishment"**: that is, difficult and harsh.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is a mountain in Hell, which they are made to climb; whenever they place their hands on it, it melts." And from Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning is "a hardship of punishment." This is known in the language: *al-sa'ad* is hardship. One says: "The matter made me climb (*tasa'-'adani*)" when it was difficult for you, and from this is the saying of 'Umar: "Nothing has ever made me climb (*ma tasa'-'adatni*) as the marriage proposal did," that is, nothing was as difficult for me.

And "a punishment *sa'ad*" means severe. *Al-sa'ad* is the verbal noun of *sa'ida* (to ascend); one says: "He ascended, *sa'adan* and *su'udan*," so it is described as a punishment, because it overpowers the one being punished, that is, it rises over him and prevails over him, so he cannot bear it. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-sa'ad* is a verbal noun, meaning "a punishment possessing *sa'ad*," and walking uphill is difficult. *Al-su'ud* is the steep climb.

'Ikrimah said: "It is a smooth rock in Hell, whose ascent is imposed upon him. When he reaches its top, he is sent down into Hell." Al-Kalbi said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah will be commanded to climb a mountain in the Fire, made of smooth rock. This is the meaning of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I will overburden him with a severe ascent﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17].

This is understood as a matter of revelation, meaning: it was revealed to me that if they had remained upright.

Ibn Bahr mentioned: everything in this surah that has the heavy, kasrah-marked *inna* is a report of the words of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an and then returned to their people as warners. Everything in it that has the light, fatha-marked *anna* is revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The poet said:

*"Indeed, by Allah, if only I were free,*
*and you are neither free nor a freed slave."*

Whoever reads with fatha the letter before the light *an* (the *anna* of revelation), makes it coordinate with *anna hu* ("that it") after "it was revealed to me," and *wa-an law istaqamu*, or with "we believed in it and in that if they had remained upright." Whoever reads all the particles with kasrah up to the light *an* may coordinate the light *an* with "it was revealed to me" or with "we believed in it," and dispense with implying an oath.

The reading of the majority (*qira'at al-'ammah*, the standard recitation) is with kasrah on the *waw* of *law* because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Wththab and al-A'mash read it with a *damma* on the *waw*.

**First issue:** Concerning His saying, ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah﴾, *anna* with a fatha. It was said that it refers back to His saying, ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], meaning: "Say: It has been revealed to me that the mosques belong to Allah." Al-Khalil said: meaning "and because the mosques belong to Allah." The intended meaning is the houses that the adherents of the religions build for worship.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The jinn said, "How can we go to the mosques and attend the prayer with you, when we are far from you?" So this was revealed: ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah﴾, meaning they were built for the remembrance of Allah and for obeying Him.

Al-Hasan said: By it He means all places, because the whole earth is a mosque for the Prophet (ﷺ). He says: "Wherever you are, pray," and: "Wherever you pray, that is a mosque." In the Sahih: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Talq ibn Habib said: By the mosques He means the limbs with which the servant prostrates, namely the two feet, the two knees, the two hands and the face. He says: "These are the limbs with which Allah has blessed you, so do not prostrate to anyone else with them, lest you deny the blessing of Allah."

Ata said: "Your mosques are your limbs with which you were commanded to prostrate; do not humble them before anyone other than their Creator."

In the Sahih, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I was commanded to prostrate upon seven bones: the forehead" — and he pointed with his hand to his nose — "and the two hands, the two knees, and the tips of the two feet."

Al-Abbas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the servant prostrates, seven *araab* prostrate with him." [*Araab*: limbs; its singular is *irb*, with a kasra and then sukun.]

It was also said: The mosques are the prayers, meaning because prostration is to Allah. This was also said by al-Hasan.

If you take *al-masajid* to mean the places, its singular is *masjid* with a kasra on the *jim*, and it is also said with a fatha; this was related by al-Farra'. If you take it to mean the limbs, its singular is *masjad* with a fatha on the *jim*.

It was also said: It is the plural of *masjad*, which means prostration. One says: "I prostrated (*sajadtu*) a prostration (*sujudan*) and a *masjad*," just as one says: "I struck upon the earth a striking (*darban*) and a *madrab* with a fatha," meaning when one travels in search of provision.

Ibn Abbas said: "The mosques here means Makkah, which is the qibla, and Makkah was called *the mosques* because everyone prostrates towards it."

The first opinion is the most apparent of these opinions, if Allah wills, and it is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah have mercy on him.

**Second issue:** His saying, ﴿Allah's﴾, is an idafa of honour and dignity. Then He singled out from among them the Ancient House, saying: ﴿Purify My House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26].

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Riding beasts are not to be made to travel except to three mosques," the hadith which the imams have transmitted. The discussion of it has already passed.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) also said: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other place, except the Masjid al-Haram." Ibn al-Arabi said: "It has been related through a chain that is not objectionable that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other place, except the Masjid al-Haram, for a prayer in it is better than a hundred prayers in this mosque of mine.' [The word *hadha* is missing from the printed original.] If this is authentic, it would be explicit."

I say: It is authentic, by the transmission of a trustworthy narrator from a trustworthy narrator, as I have explained in the surah of *Ibrahim*. [See vol. 9, p. 371.]

**Third issue:** The mosques, although they belong to Allah as ownership and honour, may also be attributed to others for identification, so it is said: "the mosque of So-and-so." In the sound hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) held races between horses that had been trained, from al-Hafya, and their finish line was Thaniyat al-Wada'. He also held races between horses that had not been trained, from Thaniyat to the mosque of Bani Zurayq.

This attribution may be by virtue of locality, as if it were in their direction of prayer; and it may be by their endowment (*tahbis*). There is no disagreement among the community concerning the endowment of mosques, bridges and graveyards, though they differ concerning the endowment of other things.

**Fourth issue:** Although the mosques belong to Allah, and nothing is mentioned in them except Allah, it is permissible to divide wealth within them. It is permissible to place charitable gifts in them as a common stock among the poor, and whoever comes eats. It is permissible to detain a debtor in them, to bind a captive in them, to sleep in them, for a sick person to dwell in them, to open the door for the neighbour (*al-jar*) to come to them, and to recite poetry in them if it is free of falsehood. [So in Ibn al-Arabi. In the printed edition: "for the passer-by (*lil-mar*) to come to them."] All of this has already passed, explained in the surah of *Bara'a* [see vol. 8, p. 104] and *al-Nur* [see vol. 12, p. 265] and others.

**Fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿So do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾. This is a rebuke of the polytheists for invoking other than Allah alongside Him in the Masjid al-Haram.

Mujahid said: When the Jews and Christians entered their churches and synagogues, they associated partners with Allah, so Allah commanded His Prophet and the believers to make the invocation purely for Allah whenever they enter all the mosques. He says: "Do not associate with Him in them an idol or anything else that is worshipped." [This is as in all the originals; he means: "or anything else."]

It was also said: The meaning is: Reserve the mosques for the remembrance of Allah, do not take them as a mockery, a marketplace, a meeting place, or a thoroughfare, and do not make any share in them for other than Allah.

In the Sahih: "Whoever announces a lost item in the mosque, say to him: May Allah not return it to you, for the mosques were not built for this."

What is sufficient of the rulings on mosques has already passed in the surah of *al-Nur*, and all praise is due to Allah.

**Sixth issue:** Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that when he entered the mosque he would put forward his right foot, and he would say: "﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ O Allah, I am Your servant and Your visitor, and every visited one has a right, and You are the best of those visited. So I ask You, by Your mercy, to free my neck from the Fire." When he went out of the mosque, he would put forward his left foot, and he would say: "O Allah, pour upon me goodness abundantly, do not withdraw from me the good You have given me ever, do not make my livelihood toil, and make for me in the earth *jadd*." [*Jadd*, with a fatha: fortune and wealth, as in *al-Lisan*.] That is, wealth.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 72, verses 19–21:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that when the servant of God stood up calling upon Him﴾. The word *anna* (that) may be read with a fath (*anna*), meaning that God revealed to him that... It may also be read with a kasra (*inna*), as a new sentence (*isti'naf*). "The servant of God" here refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) when he was praying in the valley of Nakhla (*Batn Nakhla*) [in the Taj al-Arus: "Nakhla" is a place between Mecca and Ta'if, and it is also called *Batn Nakhla*], and reciting the Qur'an, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah. "Calling upon Him" means worshipping Him. Ibn Jurayj said: "Calling upon Him" means that he stood up among them calling to God, the Exalted.

(﴿They were almost crowding upon him﴾.) Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam said: They are the jinn, when they listened to the Qur'an from the Prophet (ﷺ). That is, some of them almost mounted upon others out of crowding, and they fell down, out of eagerness to hear the Qur'an. It is also said: "They almost mounted him out of eagerness," as al-Dahhak said. Ibn Abbas said: out of desire to hear the remembrance (*dhikr*). Bard narrated from Makhul that the jinn pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on this night, and they were seventy thousand, and they finished giving their pledge at the break of dawn. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas: this is from the saying of the jinn when they returned to their people and told them what they had seen of the obedience of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their following him in bowing and prostration. It is also said: the meaning is that the polytheists almost mounted one another out of rage against the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: meaning, when Muhammad, the servant of God, stood up with the call, the humans and the jinn banded together against this matter in order to extinguish it, but God refused except to support him and perfect His light. Al-Tabari preferred that the meaning be: the Arabs almost gathered against the Prophet (ﷺ) and banded together to extinguish the light which he had brought.

Mujahid said: His saying *libadan* means groups, and it is from *talabbud al-shay' 'ala al-shay'*, that is, gathering together. From it comes *al-libad*, which is spread out (as a carpet) because of the accumulation of its wool [in manuscripts A and H: "*suffuhu*" (its rows); in T: "*safhu*"]. Anything you stick firmly to something is *labbadtahu*. The plural of *al-libdah* is *libad*, like *qirbah* and *qirab*. The hair on the back of a lion is called *libdah*, and its plural is *libad*. Zuhayr said:

*Near a lion, armed, hurling (his prey), whose claws are not trimmed, with a mane...*

Locusts in great numbers are also called *libad*. It has four dialects and readings: the *ba'* with a fath and the *lam* with a kasra, which is the reading of the common people. The *lam* with a damma and the *ba'* with a fath, which is the reading of Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Hisham from the people of Syria; its singular is *lubdah*. And with a damma on the *lam* and the *ba'*, which is the reading of Abu Haywah, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa, Abu al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Jahdari; its singular is *labd*, like *saqf* and *suquf*, *rahn* and *ruhun*. And with a damma on the *lam* and a shadda on the *ba'* with a fath, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliyah, al-A'raj and al-Jahdari also [the word "also" is omitted in manuscripts A, Z, H and T]; its singular is *labbad*, like *raki'* and *rukka'*, and *sajid* and *sujjad*. It is also said: *lubad* with a damma on the *lam* and a fath on the *ba'* means "that which is lasting," and from it the vulture of Luqman is called *Labad*, because of its enduring and lasting. Al-Nabigha said:

*Time has consumed them, as it consumed Labad.*

Al-Qushayri said: It was also read *lubudan* with a damma on the *lam* and the *ba'*, and it is the plural of *labid*, which is the small *juwaliq* [in the originals: "*al-Jawlaq*" is a distortion]. In the Sihah: [and His saying, the Exalted] "I have squandered wealth in abundance" (*malan labadan*), that is, much. It is also said: the people are *lubad*, that is, gathered together. *Al-lubad* also means one who does not travel and does not leave his dwelling [*manzilahu*; the addition is from Lisan al-Arab, entry *labd*]. The poet said:

*From a man of generosity, to whom there is always a fully ripe judgment, by which the stationary one is outdone, the one who remains (*al-lubad*)...*

It is also narrated as *al-labid*. Abu Ubayd said: this is closer [to correct]. [*Al-bazla'* is the good opinion. So-and-so is *nahhad* with *bazla'* when he is one who handles great matters. The poet said:

*When the gaps of a people occupy me, I am one of wide paths, one who rises up with a sound judgment.*

What is between the brackets is missing from A, H, W and T.] *Labad* is also the last of the vultures of Luqman, and it is declinable, because it is not an irregular form. The Arabs claim that Luqman was the one whom 'Ad sent in their delegation to the Sacred Precinct (*al-Haram*) to ask for rain for them. When they were destroyed, Luqman was given a choice between the survival of seven *ba'arat* [the commentator of the Qamus said: it is with an 'ayn, and in some copies of the Sihah it is "*baqarat*" with a qaf; but what is in the copies of the Qamus is closer, since cattle are not born from gazelles], [i.e., seven] dark-colored cows of oryx, in a rugged mountain, which rain does not touch, or the survival of seven vultures, each time one vulture died another vulture succeeded it. He chose the vultures, and the last of his vultures was called *Labad*, and the poets mentioned it. Al-Nabigha said:

*Its dwelling-places became empty, and its people departed; time has consumed them, as it consumed Labad.*

*Al-Labid* is the small *juwaliq*; it is said: "I put the waterskin into a *labid*." *Labid* is also the name of a poet from Banu 'Amir.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾. That is, he (ﷺ) said: "I only call upon my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with Him." Thus most of the reciters read *qala* (he said) as a report. Hamzah and 'Asim read *qul* (say) as a command. The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to him: "You have brought a great matter, and you have opposed all the people. So turn back from this, and we will protect you." Then the saying of God, the Exalted, was revealed: ﴿Say: I have no power to bring you harm or good﴾, that is, I am not able to repel from you harm or drive to you good. It is also said: "I have no power to bring you harm" means disbelief, "or good" means guidance, that is, my duty is only to convey. It is also said: "harm" is punishment, and "good" is blessing; and this is the first meaning itself. It is also said: "harm" is death, and "good" is life.

He drew a line around me, then went forward toward them, and they crowded around him. A chief of theirs called Wardan said, 'I will push them away from you.' He said: ﴿No one can protect me from Allah.﴾" This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. He said: "It may have two meanings. The first: no one can protect me alongside Allah's protection. The second: no one can protect me from what Allah has decreed for me."

﴿Nor will I find any refuge other than Him﴾: that is, any place of refuge (multaja') to which I may turn. This is the view of Qatadah. It is also reported from him that it means helper and protector. Al-Suddi said it means a shelter (hirz). Al-Kalbi said it means an entrance into the earth like a tunnel (sarab). It is said it means a guardian and no protector, and it is said it means a way of escape and no path. This was related by Ibn Shajarah. The meaning is one, and from it is the verse of the poet:

*"Alas for my soul, and alas, a lament that avails me nothing,*
*and there is no refuge from the decree of Allah."*

It is also said that it is a verbal noun (masdar), and "la" here means "lam," and "in" is conditional. The meaning would be: "I will not find any refuge other than Him, if I do not convey the messages of my Lord in conveyance."

**Issue 1:** Concerning this there are two questions. The first is His saying, ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. "Knower" is in the nominative as a description (na't) of "my Lord" in His saying, ﴿My Lord﴾. It was also said that the meaning is: He is the Knower of the unseen, and the unseen is what is hidden from the servants. Its explanation has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 163.]]. ﴿So He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger He has chosen. For indeed, He makes it known to him what He wills of His unseen, because the messengers are supported by miracles, and among them is the reporting of some hidden matters. In the Revelation [[See vol. 4, p. 95.]] there is: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 49]. Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿except a messenger He has chosen﴾ refers to Jibril, peace be upon him. But this is far-fetched. The better meaning is: He does not reveal His unseen to anyone except the one He has chosen, that is, selected for prophethood. Then He makes him aware of what He wills of His unseen, so that this serves as evidence of his prophethood.

**Issue 2:** The scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: When He praised Himself with knowledge of the unseen and singled it out for Himself apart from His creation, this was evidence that no one other than Him knows the unseen. Then He excepted those among the messengers whom He has chosen, entrusting to them what He wills of His unseen through revelation to them, and making it a miracle for them and a true sign of their prophethood. The astrologer (al-munajjim, one who practices tanjīm, astrology) and those like him, who cast pebbles, look into books, and divine by birds, are not among those whom He has chosen from among the messengers so that He makes them aware of what He wills of His unseen. Rather, he is a disbeliever in God, one who fabricates against Him by his conjecture, guesswork, and lying. One of the scholars said: "I wonder what the astrologer would say about a ship in which a thousand people board, with differing conditions and varying ranks, among them the king and the commoner, the scholar and the ignorant, the rich and the poor, the old and the young, along with differing ascendants, varying birth-times, and different positions of their stars, and then they all are overtaken by drowning in a single hour?" If the astrologer, may God curse him, says: "It was only the ascendant under which they boarded that drowned them," then it would follow from that that this ascendant nullified the judgments of all those ascendants, despite their differences, at the birth of each one of them, and what their particular ascendant requires. Then there would be no benefit at all in casting horoscopes, and no indication in them of a wretched or a happy person, and nothing would remain but opposition to the Mighty Qur'an. In this there is also the permission to shed his blood on account of this astrology. The poet spoke well when he said:

*The astrologer ruled that my birth-ascendant*
*Decrees for me a death by drowning.*

*Say to the astrologer, "By the morning of the Flood, was everyone born under the star of drowning?"*

It was said to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, when he intended to meet the Khawārij: "Will you meet them while the moon is in Scorpio?" He, may God be pleased with him, said: "Then where is their moon?" And that was at the end of the month. So look at this word with which he replied, and at the strong refutation it contains against whoever holds to astrology, and at the confounding of every ignorant person who affirms the judgments of the stars.

Musāfir ibn ʿAwf said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful! Do not march in this hour, but march in three hours that will pass from the day." ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said to him: "And why?" He said: "If you march in this hour, a calamity and severe harm will befall you and your companions. But if you march in the hour I have commanded you, you will be victorious, you will prevail, and you will attain what you seek." ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "There was no astrologer for Muhammad (ﷺ), and there is none for us after him," from a long speech in which he argues with verses from the Revelation. "Whoever believes you in this statement, I am not safe for him from becoming like one who has taken rivals or equals besides God. O God, there is no omen except Your omen, and no good except Your good." Then he said to the speaker: "We disbelieve you, we oppose you, and we will march in the hour you forbid us." Then he turned to the people and said: "O people, beware of learning the stars except what guides you in the darknesses of land and sea. The astrologer is only like the sorcerer, the sorcerer is like the disbeliever, and the disbeliever is in the Fire. By God, if I hear that you look into the stars and act upon them, I will imprison you for as long as you and I remain, and I will deprive you of your allowance for as long as I have authority." Then he marched in the hour he had forbidden, met the people, and killed them. This is the battle of al-Nahrawān, which is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim. Then he said: "If we had marched in the hour he commanded us, and we had been victorious and prevailed, a sayer would have said: 'He marched in the hour the astrologer commanded him.' There was no astrologer for Muhammad (ﷺ), and there is none for us after him. God opened to us the lands of Kisrā and Caesar and all the other lands." Then he said: "O people! Rely upon God and put your trust in Him, for He suffices against whoever is other than Him."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may know﴾. Qatadah and Muqatil said: meaning, that Muhammad may know that the messengers before him had indeed conveyed the message just as he conveyed the message. There is an omission to which the lam is attached, meaning: We informed him by Our preserving the revelation, so that he may know that the messengers before him were in the same condition as his, conveying with truth and sincerity. It was also said: that Muhammad may know that Jibril and those with him had conveyed the message of his Lord to him; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. He said: Revelation never descended except with four guardians from among the angels, peace be upon them. It was also said: that the messengers may know that the angels conveyed the messages of their Lord. It was also said: that the Messenger may know, whichever messenger he was, that the messengers other than him had conveyed. It was also said: meaning, that Iblis may know that the messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord intact, free from his confusion and the eavesdropping of his companions. Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, that the jinn may know that the messengers had conveyed what was revealed to them, and that they were not the ones conveying it through eavesdropping on them. Mujahid said: that whoever denied the messengers may know that the messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord. The reading of the majority is ﴿liya'lama﴾ with a fatha on the ya', and its interpretation is what we have mentioned. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Humayd and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ya', meaning: that he may make people know that the messengers had conveyed. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, that Allah may know that His messengers had conveyed His messages, with a fatha on the ya', like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has not yet known those of you who strive, nor known the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]. The meaning: that Allah knows that with the knowledge of witnessing, just as He knew it unseen.

(﴿And He has encompassed what is with them﴾) meaning: His knowledge has encompassed what is with them, that is, what is with the messengers and what is with the angels. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning: that the messengers may know that their Lord's knowledge has encompassed what is with them, so that they convey His messages.

(﴿And He has enumerated everything in number﴾) meaning: He has encompassed the number of everything, known it and known it, so nothing of it is hidden from Him. ''Adadan'' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: He has enumerated everything in the state of being counted. If you wish, it may be read as a verbal noun, meaning: He has enumerated and counted everything with a counting, so it is the verbal noun of the omitted verb. He, glorified is He, is the All-Enumerating, the All-Encompassing, the All-Knowing, the Guardian of everything. We have explained all of this in the book "al-Kitab al-Asna, fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna" (The Most Excellent Book, on the Explanation of Allah's Beautiful Names). And praise belongs to Allah alone.
